claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength compared with some other high-entropy alloys.
The relatively low hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi are caused by its homogeneous single-phase solid-solution state and the associated absence of nanoscale precipitates or phase separation.
Nanoscale precipitates or phase-separated regions can provide additional strengthening in high-entropy alloys.
Second phases strengthen alloys by impeding dislocation motion.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi material is an equimolar or nearly equimolar, homogenized, single-phase FCC or BCC solid solution.
Single-phase CoCrFeNiTi exhibits high ductility and machinability.
Controlled aging can induce nanoscale precipitation or slight phase decomposition in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi without excessive grain growth.
A fine dispersion of nanoscale precipitates or a second phase would act as a barrier to dislocation motion.
Precipitates or decomposed phases pin dislocations.
Precipitate or phase strengthening raises hardness and yield strength.
In the homogeneous solid solution, dislocations move relatively unimpeded, causing lower hardness and strength.
The absence of precipitates improves plasticity relative to a precipitate-strengthened state.
Aged CoCrFeNiTi samples that develop nanoscale precipitates will have higher hardness and yield strength than the as-solid-solution baseline.
Precipitate-bearing aged CoCrFeNiTi will have lower ductility than the as-solid-solution baseline.
Dislocation-based deformation mechanisms dominate in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi from room temperature through 600 °C.
Above 600 °C, dynamic recovery or recrystallization may overshadow precipitate strengthening.
The proposed comparison is limited to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested at 25 °C and up to 600 °C under tensile or compressive elastic-plastic loading.

contradictions.description: The predicted strengthening is conditional on successful precipitate formation, but the falsification rule treats failure of the aging treatment to form precipitates as falsification of the strengthening mechanism. Failure to create the proposed mediator would instead make the mechanical comparison inconclusive.
